eutrophication-s1.title: A lake through one summer after heavy fertilizer runoff

plot.label: Dual-axis line graph over 12 weeks in a lake: algae, measured as chlorophyll in micrograms per liter, rises from 5 to a peak of 60 at week 5 and falls to 15; dissolved oxygen in the deep water stays near 8 milligrams per liter until week 5 then falls to 1 by week 8 and recovers slowly to 5; invented data

eutrophication-s2.title: Phosphorus and algae in five lakes

table.caption: Total phosphorus and summer algae in five lakes in one region (invented data for practice)

items.q: When does bottom dissolved oxygen fall fastest?
options: Weeks 0 to 3, as the algae begin to grow
Weeks 5 to 8, just after the algae peak
Weeks 10 to 12, at the end of the summer
Weeks 3 to 5, while the algae are growing fastest

why.correct: DO drops from 6.5 to 1.0 mg per L between weeks 5 and 8, just after the algae peak at week 5, when the algae are dying.
options: DO barely changes then, from 8.2 to 7.8.
Right: DO falls from 6.5 to 1.0 as the bloom dies back.
DO is rising again then, from 2.8 to 5.0.
DO falls only a little then; the steep drop comes after the peak.

items.q: Why does the steep drop in bottom DO come after the algae peak rather than during the growth of the bloom?
options: Decomposers use oxygen breaking down dead algae
Living algae breathe in most of the oxygen as they grow
Fertilizer reacts with oxygen and removes it directly
The water warms in late summer and boils off the oxygen

why.correct: While algae grow they make oxygen near the surface. When they die, they sink, and decomposers break them down using oxygen from the deep water. So DO falls as the bloom dies.
options: Right: decomposition of the dying bloom uses up the oxygen.
Growing algae make oxygen by photosynthesis near the surface.
Nitrate and phosphate do not remove oxygen themselves.
Warming lowers DO somewhat, but it does not explain the timing after the peak.

items.q: Find the percent change in bottom DO from week 0 to week 8.

mistakes.why: You divided by the week 8 value. Divide by the starting value, 8.2 mg per L.
DO fell, so the change is negative: about -87.8%.

items.q: A fish kill was reported in week 8. Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: The fertilizer itself poisoned the fish
Algae clogged their gills at the bloom's peak
Cold late-summer water killed the fish
Low oxygen after the bloom died killed them

why.correct: At week 8 bottom DO reached 1.0 mg per L, far below what most fish need (about 5 mg per L), so the fish likely died from hypoxia caused by decomposition of the bloom.
options: The graph points to oxygen, not direct poisoning by nutrients.
The kill came three weeks after the algae peak, when DO was lowest.
Nothing in the graph shows cold water.
Right: DO hit 1 mg per L at week 8.

items.q: What relationship do the five lakes show between phosphorus and algae?
options: More phosphorus goes with less algae
Phosphorus and algae are not related
More phosphorus goes with more algae
Algae are highest in the forest lakes

why.correct: Lakes with more phosphorus have more algae: from 8 µg per L and 2 µg per L of chlorophyll in Crystal Lake to 110 and 62 in Town Lake.
options: Town Lake has the most of both.
They rise together across all five lakes.
Right: algae rise steadily with phosphorus.
The forest lakes have the least algae.

items.q: Why does water clarity fall as phosphorus rises?
options: Phosphorus is a dark powder that stains the water
More phosphorus feeds algae that cloud the water
Clear lakes are deeper, so they hold less phosphorus
Fish stir up the bottom in lakes with more phosphorus

why.correct: More phosphorus feeds more algae, which cloud the water. Crystal Lake is clear to 7.5 m; Town Lake, green with algae, only to 0.5 m.
options: Dissolved phosphate is not what clouds the water; the algae are.
Right: clarity falls as algae rise.
Depth is not in the table; the link is through algae.
The table gives no fish data.

items.q: Which lake is most likely oligotrophic?
options: Crystal Lake, clear and low in nutrients
Town Lake, which has the most phosphorus
Corn Lake, beside fields of row crops
Mill Lake, beside grazed pasture land

why.correct: An oligotrophic lake is low in nutrients, with little algae and clear water. Crystal Lake has the least phosphorus (8), least algae (2) and clearest water (7.5 m).
options: Right: low nutrients, little algae, high clarity.
High nutrients and algae make it eutrophic, not oligotrophic.
Its high phosphorus and algae make it eutrophic.
Its phosphorus and algae are moderate to high.

items.q: How many times as much phosphorus does Town Lake have as Crystal Lake?

mistakes.why: 102 is the difference. "How many times as much" divides: 110 / 8.
You divided the smaller by the larger. Divide Town Lake (110) by Crystal Lake (8).

items.q: Put the steps of cultural eutrophication in order.
options: Nitrate and phosphate from fertilizer or sewage enter a lake
The extra nutrients cause an algal bloom
Algae block sunlight, and plants below and algae die
Decomposers break down the dead matter, using oxygen
Dissolved oxygen falls (hypoxia)
Fish and other animals die or leave

why.correct: Nutrients, bloom, die-off, decomposition, oxygen drop, fish kill: every link named.

options: Pesticides sprayed on crops
Heat from power plant cooling water
Sulfur dioxide from coal plants
Nitrogen and phosphorus nutrients

why.correct: Nutrients, mainly nitrogen (nitrate) and phosphorus (phosphate) from fertilizers, manure, sewage and some detergents, cause eutrophication. Pesticides do not.
options: Pesticides kill pests; they do not feed algae. This is a common mix-up.
Heat is a different problem, covered in the next topic.
SO2 causes acid deposition, not eutrophication.
Right: extra nutrients feed the bloom.

items.q: Why does adding phosphorus to a freshwater lake so often cause an algal bloom?
options: Phosphorus kills the fish that eat algae
Phosphorus warms the water so algae grow faster
It is usually the limiting nutrient there
Phosphorus raises the pH so algae live longer

why.correct: Phosphorus is usually the limiting nutrient in fresh water: it is the one in shortest supply, so adding it removes the limit on algal growth.
options: Phosphorus at these levels does not kill fish directly.
Phosphate does not warm water.
Right: adding the scarce nutrient releases growth.
Algae still die; that is part of the problem.

items.q: Which actions would cut the nutrients reaching a lake fed by farm runoff? Select all that apply.
options: Plant buffer strips of grass and trees along the shore
Switch to a different insecticide on the fields
Pump air into the lake bottom each summer
Add a chemical to the lake that kills the algae

why.correct: Only the buffer strips keep nitrate and phosphate on the land. Aerating the lake and killing the algae treat symptoms while the same nutrients keep arriving, and insecticides are pesticides, not nutrients.
options: Right: plants take up nitrate and phosphate from runoff before it reaches the lake.
Insecticides are pesticides, not nutrients; changing them does not cut nitrate or phosphate.
Aeration raises oxygen but treats a symptom; the same nutrients still arrive.
Killing the bloom does not cut the nutrients, and the dead algae still decompose and use oxygen.

items.q: Where does the Gulf of Mexico dead zone come from?
options: Oil leaking from drilling platforms in the Gulf
Nutrients carried down the Mississippi
Warm water from Gulf power plants
Acid rain falling on the Gulf

why.correct: Nitrogen and phosphorus from farms and cities across the huge Mississippi River watershed flow to the Gulf each spring and summer, feeding blooms whose decomposition creates hypoxic bottom water.
options: Oil spills cause other harm; the dead zone comes from nutrients.
Right: a nonpoint source spread over a vast watershed.
Warm discharge is local; the dead zone is fed by river nutrients.
Acid rain does not create hypoxic dead zones.

items.q: Complete the cause-and-effect chain that explains how fertilizer runoff causes a fish kill.

why.correct: A complete chain names every link: nutrients, bloom, die-off, decomposition using oxygen, low DO, fish death. Skipping decomposition is the most common lost point.

specific.frame: Fertilizer adds nutrients, which cause ___; when the algae die, ___, so ___ and fish die.

bloom.label: First effect
options: an algal bloom
the water to cool
the fish to grow faster

why.1: Nutrients do not cool the water.
why.2: Nutrients feed algae, not fish directly.

decomp.label: What happens to the dead algae
options: decomposers break them down and use up oxygen
they turn into fertilizer and float away
sunlight dissolves them

why.1: Dead algae sink and decompose; they do not float away as fertilizer.
why.2: Sunlight does not dissolve dead algae.

result.label: Result
options: dissolved oxygen falls
the water becomes acidic
the lake gets deeper

why.1: The key change is oxygen, not acidity.

specific.model: Fertilizer adds nutrients, which cause an algal bloom; when the algae die, decomposers break them down and use up oxygen, so dissolved oxygen falls and fish die.

items.q: A 200-hectare farm applies 150 kg of nitrogen fertilizer per hectare. Studies suggest 20% runs off to a nearby stream. Write the setup for the kilograms of nitrogen that run off, then the answer.

mistakes.why: That is all the fertilizer applied. Multiply by 20 / 100 for the share that runs off.
Divide the 20 by 100 to turn the percent into a fraction.
30,000 kg is the total applied. 20% of it runs off: 6,000 kg.
You used 20 instead of 20 / 100. Divide the percent by 100.

items.q: Write a testable hypothesis for an experiment on how phosphate affects algae in pond-water tanks.

why.correct: It names the change (more phosphate), the measured variable (algae, as chlorophyll), a direction (increase) and a reason (phosphorus is limiting).

iv.label: Independent variable
options: more phosphate is added to the tanks
the tanks are painted blue
more fish are added

why.1: Tank color is not the variable being tested.
why.2: Fish are not the variable being tested.

dv.label: Dependent variable
options: the amount of algae (chlorophyll)
the air temperature in the lab

why.1: Air temperature should be kept constant, not measured as the result.

dir.label: Direction
options: increase
be affected

why.1: "Be affected" gives no direction; say increase or decrease.

because.label: Reason
options: phosphorus is the limiting nutrient for algae in fresh water
phosphate makes the water colder

specific.model: If more phosphate is added to the tanks, then the amount of algae will increase, because phosphorus is the limiting nutrient for algae in fresh water.
